description: Master the Period Study extended essay — substantiated judgement, factor weighting and change over time.
content_html:
Understanding the 16-Mark Period Essay

The 16-mark extended essay is the highest-tariff question in the Period Study component. It tests your ability to construct a substantiated judgement. This means more than writing a lot — examiners want you to argue a position, support it with precise evidence, acknowledge the strongest counter-arguments, and then reach a clear conclusion that answers the question directly. A student who writes three pages of description without arguing a position will cap at around the middle band.

Key Fact

A top-band 16-mark essay has three non-negotiable features: (1) An argument — your thesis stated upfront, not after several paragraphs of description. (2) Precise evidence — named dates, people, acts, statistics specific to this period. (3) A substantiated overall judgement — a conclusion that directly answers the question by weighing the evidence, not merely summarising what you’ve written.

Dissecting a Typical Question

Period essay questions follow a predictable pattern. Examples include:

  • “How far was the New Deal the main reason for America’s economic recovery?”
  • “The civil rights movement achieved more through legal action than through direct protest.’ How far do you agree?”
  • “How significant was the role of the president in bringing about change in the USA between 1929 and 2000?”

All three questions share a structure: they name one factor (or claim) and ask “how far” or “how significant.” Your job is to weigh that factor against others and reach a verdict. A common error is to agree entirely with the question’s claim: this removes the complexity the examiner is testing. Even if the named factor is genuinely the most important, you must engage with the others and explain why they are less significant.

A reliable paragraph structure is PEEL: Point (state your argument in one sentence), Evidence (specific names, dates, acts, statistics), Explanation (how the evidence supports your argument), Link (connect back to the question). For a 16-mark essay you need at least two paragraphs arguing one side, one paragraph engaging with the counter-argument, and a conclusion. Aim for three to four focused paragraphs plus introduction and conclusion in approximately 45 minutes.

Timing tip: do not spend more than 5 minutes planning, but do plan. A one-minute bullet-point plan stops you from writing yourself into a narrative summary instead of an argument. Write your thesis — your answer to the question — in the first sentence of your introduction, not the last sentence of your conclusion.

What Examiners Mean by ‘Factor Weighting’

Factor weighting means you do not just describe two causes — you argue which was more important and why. Comparison language is your friend: “Although the New Deal provided immediate relief, it was ultimately the Second World War that achieved genuine full employment because…” The phrase “because” is doing the analytical work. Avoid: “On the one hand… On the other hand…” structures that describe both sides without ever weighing them.

Key Fact

Useful analytical phrases for the 16-mark essay: “The most significant factor was… because…”; “Although X contributed to change, Y was ultimately more important because…”; “The evidence suggests that X mattered more than Y in the long term because…”; “While X achieved [specific outcome], it did not address [specific limit], which is why Y was also crucial.”

Structuring a Response: Worked Example

Question: “How far was the New Deal the main reason for economic change in the USA between 1933 and 1945?”

Thesis (first sentence): “The New Deal was a significant but ultimately incomplete cause of economic change — the Second World War proved more transformative by eliminating unemployment and doubling GDP.”

Para 1 — New Deal’s importance: Alphabet agencies (CCC employed 3 million; TVA brought electricity to rural areas; WPA employed millions on public works); Social Security Act created safety net; reduced unemployment from 25% to around 15% by 1937. But: 1937 recession when Roosevelt cut spending proved the recovery was fragile.

Para 2 — The decisive role of the war: By 1944 unemployment below 2%. GDP roughly doubled 1939–1945. Defence production absorbed remaining unemployed. The New Deal provided relief and reform; the war delivered genuine full employment and industrial transformation. This supports the argument that the war was the main cause of economic change.

Counter-argument / concession: Without the New Deal’s banking reforms and Social Security Act, the US economic and social infrastructure might have been too damaged to sustain wartime production. The New Deal created the conditions for recovery; the war delivered it.

Conclusion: “Overall, although the New Deal was crucial in preventing total economic collapse and creating the conditions for recovery, it was the Second World War that brought decisive economic change. The New Deal mattered more for relief and structural reform; the war mattered more for economic recovery itself.”
exam_tip_html: In your exam, write your thesis in the opening sentence — not after a lengthy introduction. Examiners have many scripts to mark; stating your argument early earns credit immediately. Avoid vague openers like “There are many factors…” or “This is a complex question…” These waste time and signal narrative, not analysis. Every paragraph should have at least one precise piece of evidence (a named person, date, act, or statistic) from this period of US history.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A top-band 16-mark essay requires three things: an argument (stated upfront), precise evidence (names, dates, acts, statistics), and a substantiated overall judgement that weighs the factors and answers the question directly.
  • Factor weighting means explicitly arguing why one factor was more important than another — not just describing both sides. Use analytical connectives: “although,” “ultimately,” “in the long term,” “because” signal analysis rather than description.
  • A reliable structure: thesis in first sentence; two paragraphs of argument; one counter-argument paragraph; a focused conclusion that answers the question. Practise writing this in 45 minutes — the time pressure is real and requires planning before writing.

practice_questions.text: Write an opening thesis (2-3 sentences) for the following question: 'How far was Roosevelt's New Deal the most important turning point in the development of the USA between 1929 and 2000?'
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks awarded for a clear argument stated in first sentence; 2 additional marks for identifying at least one counter-factor and indicating the direction of the answer. Mastering: 'The New Deal was a significant turning point in expanding federal power, but the Second World War, the 1954 civil rights ruling and the 1981 Reagan revolution were all arguably more transformative depending on the theme considered — on balance, Pearl Harbor and its consequences represent the greatest turning point because they permanently changed America's global role.' Developing: A thesis that agrees entirely with the question without identifying any counter-factor.

practice_questions.text: Identify and explain two factors that caused political change in the USA between 1960 and 2000.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed factors, each with: clear identification of the factor; precise evidence; explanation of how it caused political change. e.g. (1) Watergate (1972-74) — Nixon's resignation damaged public trust in government and led to congressional reforms limiting executive power; (2) Reagan's 1980 election — a decisive ideological shift from New Deal liberalism to conservatism, reducing federal spending and cutting taxes. Secure: Two factors identified with development. Developing: One factor only or limited development. Emerging: Vague or narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'Civil rights was the most significant social change in the USA between 1929 and 2000.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs civil rights (Brown v Board 1954; Civil Rights Act 1964; Voting Rights Act 1965; end of Jim Crow) against other social changes (women's rights — Equal Pay Act 1963, Roe v Wade 1973; media transformation — TV to internet; counterculture and generational change). Must acknowledge: civil rights was profound in law but economic racial inequality persisted; therefore 'most significant' requires definition. Substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes civil rights without weighing against other changes. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which change in the USA's foreign policy between 1929 and 1945 was significant for the rest of the period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (Pearl Harbor ended isolationism permanently; USA became founding member of UN and NATO; Cold War defined foreign policy 1947-1991; nuclear deterrence became central to global security) AND develops the chain of effects from 1941 forward. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Using this question structure as your guide, write a full concluding paragraph (5-8 sentences) for the following: 'How far was economic change the main driver of political change in the USA between 1929 and 2000?'
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A conclusion that: directly answers the question; weighs at least two factors; uses precise evidence from the period; reaches a qualified judgement that addresses the 'how far' element. Should argue something like: 'Economic crises (1929 Depression, 1970s stagflation, 1990s boom) were often catalysts for political change — the Depression enabled the New Deal, stagflation enabled Reagan. However, political change also occurred independently of economics — civil rights legislation was driven by social protest rather than economic forces, and Watergate's impact on public trust had no economic cause. Overall, economics was the most consistent driver of political change but not the only one.' Secure: Answers the question with evidence but judgement less precisely balanced. Developing: Summarises arguments without reaching a clear judgement. Emerging: Describes rather than concludes.

practice_questions.text: A student argues: 'The 16-mark essay should always agree with the statement in the question because examiners set questions about the most important factors.' Do you agree with this strategy? Explain your reasoning.
practice_questions.marks: This question tests exam technique understanding. Mastering: Explains that top marks require weighing factors, not agreeing with the question's claim; that 'how far do you agree' invites a qualified response; that examiners specifically reward substantiated judgement including awareness of counter-arguments; uses examples of how counter-arguments improve rather than weaken a response. Secure: Identifies that both agreement and counter-argument are needed. Developing: Suggests agreement is fine without explanation. Emerging: Agrees with the student's flawed strategy.

knowledge_checks.q: What is a 'substantiated judgement' in a 16-mark essay?
options: A conclusion that describes what happened in chronological order
A clear overall answer supported by evidence that explicitly weighs factors
An introduction that agrees with the question
A paragraph that lists both sides without reaching a verdict

knowledge_checks.q: When should you state your thesis in a 16-mark essay?
options: In the final sentence of your conclusion
In the middle of your first paragraph
In the opening sentence of your introduction
After you have described all the evidence

knowledge_checks.q: The PEEL paragraph structure stands for: Point, Evidence, Explanation and _____.
Factor _____ means explicitly arguing why one cause was more important than another, not just describing both sides.
Match each feature to whether it belongs in a top-band essay or not:
left: 'There are many factors to consider...' opener
Thesis in first sentence with a clear argument
Three pages of description without an argument
right: Top-band — states a clear position from the start
Mid/lower band — vague opener that delays the argument

flashcard_questions.a: A clear answer to the question supported by evidence that explicitly weighs the relative importance of factors.

flashcard_questions.q: Where should your thesis appear in a 16-mark essay?
flashcard_questions.a: In the opening sentence of your introduction.
Explicitly arguing why one factor was more important than another, not just describing both sides.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the danger of an 'on the one hand / on the other hand' structure without a conclusion?
flashcard_questions.a: It describes both sides without weighing them, capping you below the top band.

flashcard_questions.q: What word signals analytical comparison in an essay?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Because' — it forces you to explain causation rather than describe events.

flashcard_questions.q: How long should you spend planning a 16-mark essay?
flashcard_questions.a: Around 5 minutes — enough for a bullet-point plan and thesis, but no more.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a counter-argument paragraph achieve in a 16-mark essay?
flashcard_questions.a: It shows you are aware of complexity and can weigh competing factors, earning the highest analytical marks.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the structural weakness of agreeing entirely with a 'how far do you agree' question?
flashcard_questions.a: It removes the complexity examiners are testing and caps the response at middle band.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of an analytical sentence starter for a 16-mark essay.
flashcard_questions.a: "Although X contributed to change, Y was ultimately more important because..."

glossary_terms.definition: A clear overall answer to the question that is supported by factual evidence and explicitly weighs the relative importance of factors — the hallmark of top-band extended responses.
A paragraph structure: Point (your argument), Evidence (specific facts), Explanation (how the evidence supports your argument), Link (how this connects to the overall question).
Explicitly comparing the relative importance of two or more factors in causing change, and arguing why one was more significant than others.
